content: The Misuse of Drugs Act in New Zealand is a national legal framework designed to regulate and control the use of drugs. This law categorizes drugs into three distinct classes, referred to as Schedules, based on the level of harm they pose to individuals and society: 1. Class A (First Schedule): This category includes substances that are considered to have a very high risk of harm. 2. Class B (Second Schedule): This classification is for drugs that are deemed to have a high risk of harm. 3. Class C (Third Schedule): Substances in this group are assessed to have a moderate risk of harm. 4. Fourth Schedule: This schedule pertains to precursor substances, which are chemicals or compounds that can be used in the production or synthesis of controlled drugs. The Expert Advisory Committee on Drugs (EACD) is responsible for making decisions regarding the classification of substances into these Schedules. These decisions are informed by rigorous scientific and medical evidence, as well as obligations arising from international treaties. New Zealand is a signatory to several international drug control treaties, including the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, the Convention on Psychotropic Substances, and the United Nations Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances. These treaties impose specific obligations on member countries to align their domestic drug control policies with international standards. New Zealand’s National Drug Policy acknowledges that these international conventions require signatory nations to amend their domestic laws whenever the United Nations classifies or reclassifies a substance under one of the aforementioned treaties. Consequently, some of the substances reviewed by the EACD are brought to their attention as a direct result of decisions made at the United Nations level.
